rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2013> the study reports its own stakeholder interviews (more than 170) in six EU countries on the adoption of remote sensing in agriculture.
rows.notes: The study is a stakeholder survey of remote sensing (satellite, UAV, aircraft) adoption and value chains in France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Slovakia and Spain. It contains no result on soil sensors, no measurement of water use or water conservation, and nothing on organic systems. The only irrigation mention is that remote-sensing-derived irrigation maps are already common for corn and some wineries in Spain (an adoption statement, not an effect on water use). Technology in the passage (soil sensors/precision irrigation) differs from the technology studied (remote sensing).

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2013> the study reports its own interview data from more than 170 stakeholders in six EU countries on remote sensing adoption.
rows.notes: No result on soil sensors or on soil fertility/soil health. The study reports adoption patterns, platforms, crops, applications (mainly vegetation indices and N prescription maps), estimated remotely sensed area, and a SWOT of adoption barriers for remote sensing. It does not measure any agronomic or soil effect, and does not address organic systems. Technology mismatch: remote sensing, not soil sensors.

notes: Conference paper (ECPA 2023) reporting a multi-country stakeholder interview study on remote sensing adoption; text appears complete. Figures 1 and 2 are referenced but not reproduced in the text. The paper is about adoption and value chains of remote sensing and provides no evidence on soil sensors, water use efficiency, or soil fertility, so both claim rows fail Q2.
